blocks.content: Recognizing examiner traps is just as crucial as mastering the syllabus content.

rows: Embeds words like 'NOT' or 'INCORRECT' inside lengthy question stems
Underline/circle key qualifiers before reading the answer choices
Uses 'Always', 'Never', or 'Only' to make statements absolute
Identify counter-examples; absolute statements are usually false
Inserts high-complexity, calculation-heavy questions early in the test
Mark and skip on Round 1; solve easy conceptual questions first

items: Circle or highlight negation words ('NOT', 'EXCEPT', 'INCORRECT') immediately during your first read of the question stem.
Treat options containing absolute terms ('strictly', 'completely', 'never') with extreme skepticism.
Avoid changing marked answers in the final 5 minutes based on panic or second-guessing without concrete logical proof.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Misreading negative qualifiers like 'NOT', 'EXCEPT', or 'INCORRECT' is the most common cause of unforced errors.
Extreme qualifiers such as 'Always', 'Never', and 'Only' frequently signal incorrect statements in objective exams.
Spending over 2 minutes on a single complex question creates a severe time-management trap that jeopardizes easier questions later.
Partial-truth traps present accurate factual information in the first half of an option while inserting a subtle falsehood at the end.
